articles.intent: Build an evidence pack before deciding what to redesign
articles.dek: A useful audit helps a team choose what to change. Collect enough evidence to explain the problem, reproduce it and separate a known defect from a question.

sections.heading: Begin with a question the evidence can answer
paragraphs: I begin with a decision the team needs to make. For example, is a delivery flow confusing because a state is missing, a label is unclear or the live service is failing?
Those explanations need different evidence. A screenshot can show wording and hierarchy; a recorded task or implementation check can show what happens after the action.

sections.heading: Collect complementary evidence

rows: How common it is across all users
Why the person acted that way
The experience of people who never contacted support
The person's understanding of the failure

sections.heading: Attach provenance to each finding
paragraphs: Capture the build or environment, role, viewport, starting state, steps and result. Add a screenshot or recording only when it helps another person inspect the observation. Remove personal and client data from the version that will be shared.

Keep the original observation separate from the interpretation. For example: the save failed and the form cleared is an observation; people will abandon because of this is a hypothesis unless further evidence supports it.

sections.heading: Use a reproducible finding format
bullets: Task: what the person was trying to do.
Observation: what actually happened and where.
Consequence: what was blocked, lost or made ambiguous.
Evidence: source, date and reproduction steps.
Confidence: confirmed, observed once or needs reproduction.
Next decision: repair, investigate, accept or redesign.

sections.heading: End with a decision-ready pack
paragraphs: Group findings by the decision they inform. Several navigation symptoms may share one naming problem; a failed integration may need an engineering repair rather than new screens. The point is to narrow the redesign question, not make the issue count impressive.

For portfolio work, be equally careful about evidence. A Figma screenshot can demonstrate a proposed hierarchy. It cannot stand in for an observed usability session or a shipped outcome. Keeping those categories separate makes both the audit and the case study more credible.

sections.heading: Follow the same task across its states
paragraphs: The Zapp driver next-stop and completion designs describe different moments. Progress toward a stop is separate from a completed handoff, and payment records are a further responsibility.
The screens help define the questions for an audit. They do not tell us that a delivery occurred. Keep the observed result and the next test attached to the same finding.

articles.intent: Run a reproducible task-based interface audit
articles.dek: Walk through a real task, include one interruption and record what stopped the person from continuing. Then choose a repair that fits the evidence.

sections.heading: Set up a real starting condition
paragraphs: A useful audit starts from a believable situation. Specify the person, their starting state, the task and the result they need. Otherwise, a neat checklist can drift into reviewing screens nobody uses in that order.
Use realistic content and record the environment. Keep the evidence close enough that someone else can repeat the same review.

sections.heading: Walk the task, then the exception

rows: Can the person identify location and purpose?
Labels, current state and entry path
Is the consequence understandable before commitment?
Are requirements and correction paths clear?
Does the interface explain what it is waiting for?
Can the person continue without losing useful work?
Is the result distinguishable from an attempt?
Saved record, confirmation or next state

sections.heading: Inspect access and alternate input
paragraphs: Repeat the core path with a keyboard and a narrow viewport. Check meaningful names, visible focus, logical order and whether fixed controls cover the current task. Review zoom and the mobile keyboard rather than treating a small screenshot as responsive verification.

For role-based software, try a direct route and an unavailable action with the correct test account. Record what the server and interface actually do; a hidden button is not evidence of authorization enforcement.

sections.heading: Review the request and its final check together
paragraphs: Zapp’s parcel screen collects what is being carried. The delivery-review design then brings pickup, recipient, parcel and a sample estimate together before payment.
I would use the pair to ask whether the customer can spot and correct a wrong detail. The static designs help define that task; the working flow needs its own check.

sections.heading: Turn the result into a bounded decision
paragraphs: Record the failure at the task level and separate confirmed behavior from a suspected cause. Preserve the conditions needed to reproduce it. Then decide whether the repair belongs in copy, layout, interaction, business rules or engineering.

The checklist is complete when it produces decisions someone can act on. It is not a certification that every state, role or assistive technology has been covered. State the tested scope and the remaining gaps explicitly.

articles.intent: Choose a defensible repair order without false numerical precision
articles.dek: Fix the problems that prevent or endanger the task first. Keep confidence visible so a strong opinion does not look like a confirmed defect.

sections.heading: Start with consequence, not the screenshot
paragraphs: A dramatic screenshot is not automatically the highest-priority finding. I start with what the problem prevents someone from doing and what a wrong action could cost them.
Then I ask how certain we are. A reproduced failure, a user report and a design hypothesis can all deserve attention, but they should not carry the same confidence.

sections.heading: Keep confidence visible

rows: Repair or explicitly accept the known consequence
Reproduce and investigate while preserving evidence
Inspect the affected task and corroborate the cause
Frame as a hypothesis or targeted review
Treat as a design choice unless a consequence is established

paragraphs: The Orkest filter-error frame is a designed scenario, not a reproduced production incident. It gives a reviewer concrete feedback and retained context to inspect. Severity still depends on the affected task, available recovery and corroborating evidence.

sections.heading: Use a repair order the team can explain
paragraphs: The Orkest filter states are a small example. A visible problem in the filter needs a specific explanation and a way forward; a spacing preference can wait if the task is blocked.
Compare the default panel with the error example, then state the repair and the check that will establish it worked. A precise next action is more useful than an impressive priority score.

sections.heading: Separate quick repair from structural work
paragraphs: An incorrect label may be a small repair with a meaningful benefit. Several inconsistent states may indicate a shared component or data-model problem. Group related symptoms before estimating fixes so the team does not repeatedly patch the same cause.

Also record dependencies. A design repair can be ready while an API contract is unresolved. That does not make the whole item complete, and it should not prevent unrelated verified repairs from moving forward.

sections.heading: Keep a decision ledger
bullets: Finding and affected task.
Observed consequence and evidence link.
Severity and confidence, recorded separately.
Proposed repair and accountable owner.
Dependency or decision that blocks progress.
Verification that will demonstrate the repair.
Reason for accepting or deferring the issue.

sections.heading: Revisit priority after learning
paragraphs: Priority is a current decision, not a permanent property of a ticket. A reproduced failure, a changed release scope or new evidence can change the order. Keep the original observation and record why the decision changed.

A good audit creates a smaller set of consequential decisions and a reliable verification path. Closing a large number of low-value tickets is not a substitute for resolving the task failures that matter.

related: Decide whether an audit is the next step

articles.intent: Decide whether to audit, repair or redesign a startup product
articles.dek: An audit is useful when the team cannot yet explain why a task is failing. When the defect is already clear, start with the repair.

sections.heading: Identify the decision you cannot yet make
paragraphs: Before proposing a redesign, name the decision the team cannot make. Are people missing a step, misunderstanding the product or running into a service problem?
If several explanations fit, a small task-based audit can help choose a direction. If a broken link or missing label is already confirmed, the team can fix it without waiting for a large study.

sections.heading: Choose a response that matches the evidence

rows: Collect evidence around the affected task
A new role or business model
Review the task and information architecture
Bound the visual work and protect existing behavior

sections.heading: Scope the audit around a consequential journey
paragraphs: For a small team, start with one important role and one end-to-end task. Include entry, input, waiting, failure and completion. Identify the integrations and account states needed to test it.

The Zapp parcel step is an example of a bounded review object. It can be inspected as part of a booking journey without pretending that a single screen explains dispatch, payment and delivery operations. A sensible scope makes those boundaries explicit.

sections.heading: Ask for a decision-ready deliverable
paragraphs: The output should contain reproducible findings, consequences, confidence, a proposed repair order and a verification plan. It should distinguish copy fixes, interaction changes, structural redesign and engineering defects.

Avoid a scope that promises a predetermined redesign regardless of what the evidence shows. An audit should be able to conclude that a smaller repair is enough, that more evidence is needed or that a part of the existing product deserves protection.

sections.heading: Do not delay urgent repairs for the perfect study
paragraphs: A clear access failure, data loss or broken critical path deserves attention while broader investigation continues. Record the original condition and test the repair. There is no need to wait for every secondary finding before addressing a verified problem.

For less certain concerns, make the next experiment small and reversible. The goal is a better product decision with a known basis, not a larger design programme justified by the existence of an audit.

sections.heading: Keep the first review small
paragraphs: The Zapp driver sequence gives a useful boundary: identify the next stop, report an issue and reach completion. The completion design below gives the review an endpoint.
That is a manageable audit question. A complete delivery platform would also involve routing, dispatch and payment services, which need separate evidence.

articles.intent: Diagnose task problems concealed by visual polish
articles.dek: A polished screen can still leave someone unsure what to do. Review the task and the states around it before deciding that the answer is more visual emphasis.

sections.heading: Ask what the person can explain
paragraphs: I ask what the person can explain after looking at the screen. What is happening, which action makes sense and what do they expect next?

If the answer is unclear, stronger color or another animation may only make the same confusion more noticeable. The missing explanation could be in the state, the content or the way the task is divided.

sections.heading: Look at the state the polished view leaves out
paragraphs: Yarsha’s populated contacts and no-contact result show why the neighboring state matters. The normal list explains the objects; the empty search needs to explain how to continue.
Both views need to feel like part of the same task. A good-looking populated screen cannot answer what happens when the person’s search finds nobody.

sections.heading: Use four small diagnostic tasks
bullets: Explain the main action before selecting it.
Find the state and next action without relying on a color cue.
Trigger one error and recover without re-entering valid work.
Reach the same result using a keyboard and a narrow viewport.

sections.heading: Distinguish motion from feedback
paragraphs: A movement or color change can signal activity without explaining the result. For a consequential action, feedback should establish whether the operation is still pending, completed, rejected or unresolved. Animation can support that explanation; it should not replace it.
Also review reduced-motion behavior. If the only way to understand a result is to follow an animated sequence, the product needs an equivalent explanation that remains usable without that sequence.

sections.heading: Repair the model before adding emphasis
paragraphs: A larger primary button will not resolve an action whose meaning is unclear. First decide the task, state and consequence. Then use the visual system to make that decision easier to read.

For portfolio review, I prefer to connect a specific screen to the decision it supports and the questions still open. An attractive interface is evidence of craft. A task-based review supplies the additional evidence needed to judge the experience.

articles.intent: Review the core task hierarchy of an operational dashboard
articles.dek: Start with the decision someone needs to make from the dashboard. Review the information, actions and exceptions against that job.

sections.heading: Start with the decision the dashboard supports
paragraphs: A dashboard is easier to evaluate when its job is specific. A creditor checking application progress needs different information from an administrator reviewing a request.
I begin with the person, the record they care about and the decision available to them. Those details make it easier to judge whether a metric, table or action belongs in the overview.

sections.heading: Review the dashboard in six passes

rows: Which workspace, module and scope am I viewing?
What requires attention before routine work?
Can I identify the object and compare relevant values?
Which search, filters and sort explain this result?
What can I do, and what changes if I do it?
What happens if data, permission or the request is unavailable?

sections.heading: Inspect one source-backed example
paragraphs: The piHub creditor design puts application details and explicit status in the same comparison view. Its value as evidence is the relationship between the record and state. Redacted sample amounts are not product performance, and the image does not verify the approval workflow.

sections.heading: Check density against the job
paragraphs: Dense views can support comparison when labels, units and identifiers are stable. A review or creation step may need a quieter hierarchy because the consequence deserves attention. Do not use whitespace as the sole measure of clarity.

At narrow widths, decide which relationships survive. A person should still be able to identify a record and reach its relevant action even if secondary columns move to a detail view. Test with realistic names and missing optional values.

sections.heading: Exercise the state, not just the layout
bullets: Load the view with no records and with no matching records.
Apply a filter, inspect a record and return.
Change the selected workspace or role.
Interrupt a request and inspect retained context.
Use a keyboard to reach search, filters and a row action.
Check whether a stale or partial result is distinguishable from a genuine zero.

sections.heading: Record a task-level conclusion
paragraphs: Summarize what the dashboard enables and which decision remains difficult. A useful conclusion might be that record status is clear but ownership is hidden, or that the next action disappears on mobile. That is more actionable than saying the dashboard needs a modern look.
Keep the tested role, data and viewport in the report. A checklist pass on one template is not evidence that every module or authorization boundary has been verified.

sections.heading: Check what changes when responsibility changes
paragraphs: The piHub application list shows progress from the creditor’s side. The administrator credit-review view below gathers the request detail and decision actions for a different role.
Use the pair to check which information each person needs and whether status language stays consistent. A shared visual style is useful, but it cannot replace a clear division of responsibility.

articles.intent: Review a software website as an evaluation journey
articles.dek: A software website should help someone understand the offer, find relevant proof and decide whether to get in touch. Review that path before polishing isolated sections.

sections.heading: Test the opening explanation
paragraphs: Give a first-time visitor a moment to read the opening, then ask what the company does and who it helps. Their explanation will tell you more than asking whether they like the design.
The public Hamro Idea demo is a concrete website reference. I would review its introduction, service paths and route to contact together.

sections.heading: Review the evaluation path

rows: Specific audience, use case and scope
An appropriate demo, documentation or contact action

sections.heading: Keep proof next to the claim
paragraphs: A screenshot is useful when it helps inspect a capability or a design decision. A logo or decorative interface image does not establish a customer result. Narrow the claim when the available evidence is narrow.

The Mokshya case concerns website communication and technical reading depth. The Splashnode case concerns a technical platform website and frontend contribution. Neither should be inflated into ownership of the underlying protocol or platform just to make a stronger sales story.

sections.heading: Review contact as the next step in the same journey
paragraphs: The historical Hamro Idea contact design keeps the first request small: name, email and message. Its surrounding navigation connects it to the service and project pages.

The layout is only part of the review. Persistent labels, useful errors and a genuine delivery result need checks in the working form. The screenshot is a historical design example with sample content.

sections.heading: Review the actual page, not only the design
bullets: Read meaningful content with scripts unavailable where feasible.
Check headings, descriptive links and image alternatives.
Use the navigation and contact path with a keyboard.
Review long headings, zoom and narrow screens.
Measure image, font and script loading with real page data.
Verify metadata, canonical URLs and the intended destination of old links.

sections.heading: Use findings to refine the offer
paragraphs: If visitors cannot identify the right service, the repair may be information architecture rather than a new hero. If the page makes unsupported claims, the repair is evidence or narrower wording. Technical SEO and performance support discovery and access; they cannot make an unclear offer useful on their own.
